prompt: How does an `n2-standard-4` running all month appear on the bill?
hint: Each vCPU and each GB is billed separately.

choices.text: As one line named n2-standard-4
choices.why: The machine type is not on the bill; its parts are.

choices.text: As vCPU hours and memory hours
choices.why: Right. Four N2 cores and sixteen gigabytes of N2 memory, hour by hour.

choices.text: As a monthly fee per machine
choices.why: Usage is billed per unit of each SKU, not as a fee per instance.

choices.text: As a share of the project's quota
choices.why: Quotas limit use; they are not what the bill counts.

prompt: The same machine type costs differently in São Paulo and in Iowa. Where on the bill does that difference live?

choices.text: In a credit applied per country
choices.why: Credits are discounts and promotions, not regional prices.

choices.text: In the project's labels
choices.why: Labels say whose a cost is, not what it costs.

choices.text: In the billing account's currency
choices.why: The currency is one per account; the prices differ by SKU.

choices.text: In the SKU, which carries the region
choices.why: Right. `N2 Instance Core running in Sao Paulo` is a SKU of its own, with its own price.

prompt: To find what one machine cost last month, what should the query filter on?
hint: Its name is not on the line.

choices.text: The labels the machine carries
choices.why: Right. The line has a SKU, a project and labels; the machine is found through the labels.

choices.text: The machine type in the service field
choices.why: The service field says Compute Engine, for every machine there is.

choices.text: The instance name in the SKU
choices.why: A SKU names what Google sells, the same for every customer.

choices.text: The usage amount, which is unique per machine
choices.why: Two machines that ran all month have the same hours.

prompt: The bill rose this month while every graph of usage stayed flat. Which line of the bill is the first to read?

choices.text: The usage of each SKU
choices.why: That is what the flat graphs already showed.

choices.text: The egress to the internet
choices.why: Traffic is usage, and usage was flat.

choices.text: The credits
choices.why: Right. A discount stopped: a trial, a promotion or a commitment ended, and the same usage went back to the full price.

choices.text: The list of enabled APIs
choices.why: A new service would have shown up as new usage.

prompt: A static external address is reserved and attached to nothing. What does the bill do with it?

choices.text: Nothing, until it is attached
choices.why: Reserving it is the use being charged.

choices.text: Releases it at the end of the month
choices.why: Nothing is released on its own; it stays and bills.

choices.text: Charges it, at a higher rate than one in use
choices.why: Right. Something kept that nobody uses is the second place to look.

choices.text: Moves it to the free tier
choices.why: The free tier does not cover idle addresses.

prompt: Put the places to look in order when a bill arrives wrong, as the section lists them.
hint: From what is running to what was switched on.
trap: Starting with traffic is the slip: it is the line no single resource explains, so it is read after the resources that do.

prompt: What does a customer have to do to receive a sustained use discount?

choices.text: Run eligible machines most of the month
choices.why: Right. Google applies it on its own, as a credit at the end of the month.

choices.text: Buy it for one year in advance
choices.why: That is a committed use discount.

choices.text: Ask for it in the billing console
choices.why: There is nothing to ask for.

choices.text: Choose E2 machines
choices.why: E2 machines receive no sustained use discount.

prompt: With the lesson's example price of 0.10 dollars an hour, what did `sud.py` bill for an N1 machine that ran the whole month?
An N1 machine runs half the month. What percentage discount does sustained use give it?
hint: The first quarter at 100%, the second at 80%.

prompt: A machine runs only office hours, about a third of the month. What does sustained use do for it?
hint: Where does the first discount begin?

choices.text: A third off, in proportion
choices.why: The discount is by tiers, and the first tier has none.

choices.text: The full 30%, because it runs every day
choices.why: The tiers count hours in the month, not days.

choices.text: Nothing, because it is stopped at night
choices.why: Stopping does not disqualify it; it just has fewer hours.

choices.text: Very little, a few percent
choices.why: Right. The first quarter is billed in full; only the hours past it earn 20% off.

prompt: Two N1 machines of the same type, in the same region, run one after the other: the first for the first half of the month, the second for the rest. What does sustained use make of them?
hint: The discount follows resources, not names.

choices.text: Two machines at 10% each
choices.why: That would be true if Google counted instances.

choices.text: One machine running all month
choices.why: Right. The combined hours reach the last tier, so the month gets the full 30%.

choices.text: No discount, since neither ran a whole month
choices.why: A month is not required; and here the hours add up anyway.

choices.text: Whichever discount the cheaper machine earned
choices.why: They are the same type, at the same price.

prompt: For N1 machines, the last quarter of the month is billed at ___ percent of the base price.
What is the difference between a committed use discount and a sustained use discount?

choices.text: The commitment is paid whether used or not
choices.why: Right. Sustained use only discounts hours that ran.

choices.text: The commitment is applied automatically
choices.why: It is bought; sustained use is the automatic one.

choices.text: Sustained use lasts three years
choices.why: Sustained use is computed each month; terms of one or three years are commitments.

choices.text: The commitment can be cancelled at the end of any month
choices.why: Neither kind of commitment can be cancelled.

prompt: The planner replaces machine series every year and moves workloads between regions, but its total use is steady. Which commitment fits?

choices.text: Resource-based, for the current series
choices.why: It would keep billing for a series the planner stopped using.

choices.text: Resource-based, one in each region
choices.why: Each would be tied to one series, and the series change.

choices.text: A flexible, spend-based one
choices.why: Right. It promises dollars an hour of Compute Engine, in any series and region.

choices.text: None; sustained use covers the same need
choices.why: Sustained use is smaller and does not reward the steady total.

prompt: Put the discounts in the order Google applies them to an hour of eligible usage.
trap: Putting sustained use first is the slip: it only ever reaches usage that no commitment covered.

prompt: A one-year commitment at 37% off covers some vCPUs that will run only half the time. Is it worth it, against on demand?
hint: It pays for itself above about 63%.

choices.text: Yes, any commitment beats on demand
choices.why: Only when enough of the promised use happens.

choices.text: No, it costs more than on demand
choices.why: Right. Paying 63% of the full price for 50% of the use costs more than paying on demand for the half that runs.

choices.text: Yes, the unused half is refunded
choices.why: A commitment is paid whether used or not.

choices.text: Yes, sustained use is added on top
choices.why: Discounts are mutually exclusive.

prompt: Match each discount to what earns it.

pairs.right: running eligible machines most of the month
promising vCPUs and memory of one series in one region
promising dollars an hour of Compute Engine
accepting that Google may stop the machine at any moment

prompt: The planner's production database servers run every hour of the year in São Paulo, on one machine series that will not change. Above them, batch work comes and goes. What does the lesson's practice suggest?

choices.text: Commit everything at the peak for three years
choices.why: The batch would leave the commitment billing for nothing much of the time.

choices.text: Commit nothing; sustained use already gives 55%
choices.why: Sustained use tops out at 30%, on N1.

choices.text: Commit the batch, leave the servers on sustained use
choices.why: That commits the part that varies and leaves the steady part uncommitted.

choices.text: Commit the servers, leave the batch on demand
choices.why: Right. The steady floor gets a resource-based commitment; what varies keeps on demand and sustained use.

prompt: A team moves from N2 to a newer series halfway through a resource-based commitment for N2. What happens on the bill?
hint: The commitment does not care which machines use it.

choices.text: The commitment moves to the new series
choices.why: A resource-based commitment is for one series.

choices.text: The commitment is cancelled with a fee
choices.why: It cannot be cancelled.

choices.text: Nothing; the old machines' hours are carried over
choices.why: Unused commitment is not carried anywhere.

choices.text: The commitment keeps billing, covering nothing
choices.why: Right. Until it expires, while the new machines pay on demand.
